claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure consisting of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and a tendency toward brittle fracture.
A post-solidification annealing treatment can induce nanoscale coherent precipitates along the dual-phase lamellar interfaces.
An annealing temperature in the range of 600–800°C is potentially suitable for promoting the proposed precipitates.
The annealing duration should be selected according to the diffusion kinetics of the alloying elements.
The proposed precipitates form preferentially along phase boundaries within the lamellar colonies.
The coherent precipitates act as distributed dislocation absorption sites.
The precipitates interrupt dislocation pile-ups near lamellar interfaces.
Interrupting dislocation pile-ups reduces local stress intensification at the interfaces.
Reduced interfacial stress intensification delays microcrack initiation.
The nanoscale precipitates provide precipitation strengthening.
The annealed alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile elongation and reduced brittleness than the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will maintain or slightly increase ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
In the untreated alloy, dislocation pile-ups near lamellar interfaces cause local stress concentrations, early microcracking, and brittle failure at room temperature.
The intervention may apply to other eutectic high-entropy alloys having similar dual-phase lamellar structures.
The required annealing temperature and duration vary with alloy composition and initial colony-size distribution.
Overaging may coarsen the precipitates and degrade the strength-ductility balance.
